identity.title: Position: AI/ML Deepfake Research is Misaligned with AI Generated Non-Consensual Intimate Imagery (AIG-NCII)

problem.claim: AI/ML deepfake research does not adequately address AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery (AIG-NCII).

gap.claim: Existing work emphasizes viewer-centric epistemic harms and authenticity detection while largely overlooking subject-centric dignity harms affecting people depicted in AIG-NCII.

contributions.claim: Analyzes highly cited deepfake research to show how technical interventions address authenticity while largely ignoring AIG-NCII.
Argues for subject-centered threat models and inclusion of AIG-NCII in AI safety research, with safety guardrails and partnerships with sexual-violence-prevention experts.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that their landscape analysis finds technical deepfake interventions almost entirely ignore AIG-NCII and thereby limit the ecosystem to authenticity detection tools.
The authors report that recognizing an image as synthetic does not mitigate harms to subjects and may sometimes exacerbate them.

narrative_sequence.summary: AIG-NCII is inadequately addressed in AI/ML deepfake research.
The field prioritizes epistemic harms involving truth and authenticity, misaligning with dominant generative-AI abuse involving sexualized imagery.
A landscape analysis of highly cited work is used to characterize the near-total omission of AIG-NCII from technical interventions.
The paper contrasts viewer-centric dignity-blind interventions with subject-centric harms, then recommends updated threat models, AI-safety attention, guardrails, and expert partnerships.

source_observation.claim: The paper distinguishes harms to viewers concerning authenticity from harms to subjects concerning dignity, and argues that synthetic-image detection may not reduce the latter.

lessons.interpretation: Separating affected parties and harm types can reveal when a technically relevant intervention targets the wrong outcome.
lessons.application: Frame a research problem by mapping each intervention to its affected stakeholder and intended harm reduction, then identify uncovered subject-centered harms.
lessons.exception: This framing may be insufficient when the task genuinely concerns only provenance, authenticity, or viewer decision-making.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the landscape-analysis corpus, inclusion criteria, or operational meaning of “almost entirely.”
The conditions under which synthetic-image recognition exacerbates harm are not described.
Specific guardrails, partnership structures, and recommended technical interventions are not detailed.
